title.en: Big Neck, the Giant of the Susquehanna

region.en: Susquehanna River, Oneida fort country (traditional Tuscarora geography)
region.zh: 蘇克漢納河，奧奈達堡之地（塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理）

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: A woman on the Susquehanna bears a male child of uncommon size who beats his playmates until his mother corrects him; grown, he becomes a giant hunter named Soh-nou-re-wah, Big Neck, carrying five or six deer and bears strung on his belt, and brings home the scalps of whom he has killed. Diplomacy fails; he builds a fort on the river and ambuses travelers with a plump arrow that breaks a body in two, until three kinsmen bring him his favorite huckleberries and club him from under a cloak; he sinks in the mire and is killed.
summary.zh: 蘇克漢納河畔一婦產下巨嬰，長大後為偉大獵人，名為索努勒瓦「大頸」，腰間常掛五六隻鹿熊，並攜所殺者之髮皮。外交無效；他在河畔築堡，埋伏小徑，以能斷人為二的粗箭射殺行人。三位親族攜其最愛的越橘而來，自斗篷下以棒重擊其頭；巨人陷入泥沼，終被誅殺。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Scalp-taking is reported as the character's own attributed practice.

passages.text: On the Susquehanna a certain woman delivered a male child of uncommon size; when he was twelve years of age he was nearly as large as a grown person, and he beat his playmates, which created disputes, but his mother corrected him, and she prevailed: he promised never to injure his people. When grown up he became a giant and a great hunter, so strong that returning from hunting he would have five or six deers and bears strung round on his belt. The giant was named Soh-nou-re-wah, Big Neck, and brought several suits of dress and the scalps of whom he had killed.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Shawnees sent messengers to demonstrate his conduct, and kinsmen persuaded him to reform, but he remained only two winters without disturbance; he went down the river and committed the same outrages on every town, plundering clothes and skins. A chief offered a belt of wampum and terms of peace, which were accepted, but the giant was not disposed to favor the treaty: he built a fort on the Susquehanna, laid in ambush near the path, and shot passersby with a plump arrow so violent it would break the body in two parts.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Three warriors of his own nation brought him his favorite diet, a mess of huckleberries; while he was eating, one of the warriors, with a club concealed under his cloak, stepped on the bench and gave a fatal blow on the monster's head. So distracted, he ran from the fort intending to cross the river, but sank in the mire near the bank; the warriors prevailed and killed him on the spot. They spoiled his house and obtained a large quantity of skins, and the fort was ruined ever since.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Musqueto of Fort Onondaga

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: A great musqueto invades Fort Onondaga, flying about with a long stinger and sucking the blood of many lives; the warriors fail to expel it until the Holder of the Heavens visits the king. He chases the monster for days along the great lakes and round the country, overtakes it, and kills it near the salt lake Onondaga - and its blood becomes the small musquetos.
summary.zh: 大蚊侵擾奧農達加堡，以長針飛繞其間，吸食多人之血；戰士驅之無效，直至天堂之主拜訪國王。他沿大湖追擊怪物數日，繞行大地，終在其附近的鹽湖旁將其誅殺——其血遂化為眾多的小蚊。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. A classic etiological chase-monster; compare the Seneca mosquito slayings in Hewitt's cosmology.

passages.text: About this time a great musqueto invaded the fort Onondaga; the musqueto was mischievous to the people: it flew about the fort with a long stinger and sucked the blood of a number of lives. The warriors made several oppositions to expel the monster, but failed, and the country was invaded until the Holder of the Heavens was pleased to visit the people.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: While he was visiting the king at the fort Onondaga the musqueto made its appearance as usual and flew about the fort; the Holder of the Heavens attacked the monster. It flew so rapidly that he could hardly keep in sight of it, but after a few days' chase the monster began to fail: he chased it on the borders of the great lakes toward the sunsetting, and round the great country, until at last he overtook the monster and killed it near the salt lake Onondaga - and the blood became small musquetos.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Big Bear and the Lion of Skaneateles Lake
title.zh: 斯科尼阿特勒斯湖的大熊與獅

region.en: Skaneateles Lake near Ohiokea, west of Oneida Creek, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧奈達溪以西斯科尼阿特勒斯湖

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: In Atotarho II's day the Oyalkquoher, Big Bear, invades the hunting grounds of the five nations. Near Skaneateles lake a noise breaks out on the water: a great bear rolls stones and logs on the bank in a rage, until a lion comes out of the lake and falls upon it, beating it so that it leaves the bank. Next day the hunters find the bear; one fore leg is so heavy two men can barely lift it a hand's height, and they keep some of the meat for use in war.
summary.zh: 阿托塔霍二世時，奧雅科赫「大熊」侵擾五族獵場。斯科尼阿特勒斯湖上喧聲大作：巨熊在岸邊憤而滾落石木，直至湖中竄出獅子撲擊，將其擊退。次日獵人尋得熊屍；其前肢沉重，兩人僅能抬離地一手之高；眾人取其肉以備戰時之用。

passages.text: About this time the Oyalkquoher, or Big Bear, invaded the territory of the five nations, and the hunters were often attacked by these monsters. At the village of Ohiokea, west of Oneida creek, a small party went out to hunt and encamped near the lake Skonyatales. One morning a noise broke out in the lake; a man sent to see the tumult saw a great bear on the bank rolling down stones and logs, the monster in a great rage. A lion came out of the lake and suddenly fell upon the bear; a severe contest ensued, and the bear, beaten, was compelled to leave the bank.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day the men went in search of the bear and found it: one of the fore legs was so heavy that two men could not lift it but a hand's height. They procured some of the meat for useful purposes in the time of war.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Stonish Giant's Pointer and the Medicine Roots

region.en: Far north beyond the St. Lawrence (traditional Tuscarora geography)
region.zh: 聖勞倫斯河以北的遠方（塔斯卡洛拉傳統地理）

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: Two Onondaga beaver hunters cross the St. Lawrence into the far north; one is taken by a Stonish Giant and forced to race, faints at the giant's whoop, hides by bending a small tree and leaping among the sprouting branches of a basswood stump. The giant's 'pointer' - without which he cannot live - nearly betrays him, but the man leaps out, seizes it by the fingers, and gains the medical roots as ransom; he returns home and cures many diseases, drawing hair and worms blown in by witches.
summary.zh: 兩名奧農達加河狸獵人渡聖勞倫斯河北上；其一被石巨人擄去被迫賽跑，聞巨人呼嘯而昏倒，遂攀小樹折向他樹，藏身於萌出新椏的椴木樹樁之間。巨人賴以為生的「指針」幾乎指破行藏；獵人躍出，攫其手指奪下法器，並以藥根為贖金。他歸鄉行醫，療癒多疾，自被巫者吹入體內之人身上拔出毛髮與蠕蟲。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Bridges the giant cycle and the witchcraft cycle.

passages.text: At the Onondaga, two men went out to hunt beaver, crossed the river St. Lawrence, went far into the north, and discovered a number of beaver dams. One day a man went alone in search of beaver, but he was taken prisoner by the Stonish Giant and compelled to run a race with him. After midday the man gained and almost went out of sight, but the giant whooped, by which the man was so affected that he fainted and fell down; the giant passed him, and the man turned his course and sought to escape, climbing a small tree and bending it to another, and leaping from tree to tree until he reached a large basswood stump which had sprouted several branches, and seated himself in the midst of it.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The giant came up and examined the stump for some time, then exhibited a curious instrument which he called a pointer, possessed of a power of divination: it directed him where to find game, and the giant could not live without it. The man observed the motion of the hand, and as it was about to point to him he jumped from the stump and seized it by the fingers, instantly possessing the valuable instrument. The defeated giant entreated for the pointer and offered to mention the medical roots as a mark of friendship, which was accepted; the pointer was restored, the giant retired.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The man came home and began to doctor, and cured many diseases; he was skilled in the business and drew hair and worms from persons whom the witches had blown into their bodies. It was supposed that the Skaunvatohatihawk, the Nanticokes of the south, first founded the witchcraft: great pains were taken to procure the snakes and roots of which the stuff was made to poison the people. The witches formed a secret society, meeting in the night; when discovered they turned into foxes and wolves running swift with flashes of light, or into turkeys and big owls, or stones and rotten logs.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of Witchcraft and the Witches Burned at Onondaga
title.zh: 巫術之起源與奧農達加焚巫

region.zh: 紐約州奧農達加堡附近

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: The Nanticokes of the south are said to have founded witchcraft: a secret society gathering by night, whose members turn into foxes, wolves, turkeys or great owls to go from town to town blowing hairs and worms into bodies, and into stones or rotten logs when discovered. About fifty persons were indicted as witches and burnt to death near Fort Onondaga by order of the national committee.
summary.zh: 據說南方納提科人首創巫術：一個夜間聚會的秘密社團，其成員化為狐、狼、火雞或巨鴞往來各鎮，向人體吹入毛髮與蠕蟲；被發現時則化為石頭或朽木。約五十人被控行巫，經國族委員會之命，於奧農達加堡附近焚死。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Historicizes the Iroquois witch-belief that Parker's tales treat dramatically.

passages.text: It was supposed that the Skaunvatohatihawk, the Nanticokes in the south, first founded the witchcraft. Great pains were taken to procure the snakes and roots of which the stuff was made to poison the people. The witches formed into a secret society; they met in the night and consulted on various subjects respecting their engagements. When a person becomes a member of their society, he is forbidden to reveal any of their proceedings.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the night the witches would turn into foxes and wolves, and run very swift, attended with flashes of light; sometimes they turned into a turkey or big owl, and could fly very fast, going from town to town to blow hairs and worms into a person. If the witches were discovered by some person they turned into a stone or rotten log, entirely concealed in this situation. About fifty persons were indicted for being witches, and were burnt to death near the fort Onondaga, by order of the national committee.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Night in the Corpse House and the New Burial

region.en: Kaunehsuntahkeh, east of Oneida Creek, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧奈達溪以東考內孫塔赫

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: Returning late from hunting, a man, his wife and another shelter overnight in a house where dead bodies are deposited. When the fire dies the room darkens and something gnaws; kindling the fire, he finds the third person dead, eaten by a ghost. Fleeing with his fainting wife toward the village light, they reach safety; next day the people burn the bodies, and the five nations change their mode of burying - faces set to the east - and later alter it again when still troubled.
summary.zh: 獵罷夜歸，一男攜妻與同伴投宿於停放屍體之屋。火熄屋暗之際，忽聞啃噬之聲；重新點火後，發現同伴已死——被鬼所噬。他攜昏弱的妻子奔向村中燈火而脫險；翌日族人焚屍，五族因而改變葬俗——面朝東而葬——其後仍有擾亂，葬俗再改。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. A burial-custom aition told as ghost-story.

passages.text: Near the village of Kaunehsuntahkeh a man and his wife and another person returned from hunting, but the night was getting late before they reached the village; they went into a house where dead bodies were deposited to stay over the night. They kindled a fire and went to sleep, but when the fire was out the room became dark, and the man heard something gnawing. Kindling the fire again, he discovered the person was dead, eaten by a ghost; he trembled with fright, told his wife to quit the room as soon as possible, and followed her out.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: She became faint and could not run fast; they saw a light coming and supposed the ghost was chasing them, but fortunately gained the village. The next day the people went and burnt the dead bodies. This important event was soon made known among the five nations, and afterwards they changed their mode of burying, setting the posture face to the east; but again they were troubled with the dead bodies, and were compelled to make some alterations in burying.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: Queen Yagowanea, the Betrayal, and the Fall of the Erians
title.zh: 亞格瓦尼亞女王：背叛與伊利人之傾覆

region.en: Fort Kauhanauka (Tuscarora) and the Genesee country, New York
region.zh: 考哈農卡堡（塔斯卡洛拉）與傑納西之地，紐約州

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: Queen Yagowanea of the Erians, 'mother of the Nations,' keeps a Peace House entertaining both warring parties. When two Canandaigua warriors are smoking with her she admits a party of Messissaugers and advises them to kill her guests. A woman slips away by canoe across Lake Ontario to warn the Governor Shorihowane; his three divisions ambush the Erians behind a bear-skin decoy and slay six hundred. The great war chief Shorihowane is killed at the siege of Fort Kauquatkay, and the Queen sues for peace.
summary.zh: 伊利人的亞格瓦尼亞女王為「諸族之母」，設「和平之屋」款待交戰雙方。兩名卡南代瓜戰士正與她吸和平之菸時，她放入麥西薩格人並唆使其殺害客人。一名女子駕獨木舟渡安大略湖報信給總督肖里豪恩；總督的三個分隊以熊皮誘敵設伏，殺敵六百。大戰士肖里豪恩攻考夸特凱堡時中箭陣亡，女王乞和。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Cusick's Erian (Erie) war traditions.

passages.text: The Kanneastokaroneah or Erians sprung from the Senecas, becoming a numerous and powerful nation. A Queen named Yagowanea resided at the fort Kauhanauka; she had influence among the people and extended her authority over twelve forts. She lived outside the fort in a long house called a Peace House, entertaining the two parties who were at war with each other, and was called the mother of the Nations; each nation sent her a belt of wampum as a mark of respect. Where the Five Nations were engaged in the warfare she admitted two Canandaigua warriors into her house, and just as they began to smoke the pipe of peace, a small party of the Messissaugers came in - she betrayed her visitors, advising the Messissaugers to kill the warriors, which was soon executed.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: During the Queen's absence a woman went privately, took a canoe, and proceeded on Lake Ontario toward Canandaigua as fast as possible, going through the woods to inform the Governor Shorihowane that the Erians were making preparations to destroy the people east of the Genesee river, and directed how to send the spies. Collecting fifteen hundred warriors besides the women and old men, the governor separated the people into three divisions and marched toward the Genesee river. A warrior was dressed in a bear skin and seated on the path; the enemy chased it, which brought them into the midst of the division - at once burst a most hideous yell, followed with a rattling of war clubs. After a severe contest the Erians fled, leaving six hundred warriors slain.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The King of the Five Nations ordered the great war chief Shorihowane, a Mohawk, to march with five thousand warriors to attack the fort Kauquatkay and extinguish the council fire of the enemy. During the siege, a shower of arrows flew from the fort and the great war chief was killed; his body was conveyed back to Genesee and buried in a solemn manner, but the siege continued for several days. The Queen sued for peace; the army ceased hostilities and left the Erians entire possession of the country.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Aged Visitor Among the Tuscaroras and the Prophecy of the Whites
title.zh: 塔斯卡洛拉的年邁訪客與白人預言

region.zh: 塔斯卡洛拉聚落，北卡羅來納（傳統）

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: An aged visitor, abused by the ball-players, throws one into a tree and vanishes; returning he releases the man, teaches the people to respect their dead and love their relations, tells them the whites beyond the great water have killed their Maker but he rose again, and prophesies that the whites will one day take the Big Island and the red children 'melt away like snow before the heat.' He dies, is buried - and some who visit the grave find he has risen, never to be heard of since.
summary.zh: 一位年邁訪客遭打球者欺侮，將一人擲上樹而消失；復返後釋放其人，教眾人敬重亡者、親愛族親，並說大洋彼岸的白人殺了他們的造物主——主卻復活——又預言白人終將佔有大島，紅皮子弟「將如雪遇熱而消融」。他死後下葬；有人往墓探視，發現他已復活，自此杳無音訊。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. The Christianized prophecy is a colonial-era accretion Cusick records as tradition.

passages.text: The sixth family, the Tuscaroras, was visited by a person who went to see their amusements, but he was abused by some of the ball-players. He punished the offender by throwing him into a tree, and suddenly disappeared - but the person came again and released the fellow from the tree. The visitor appeared a very old man; he appeared among the people for a while and taught them many things: how to respect their deceased friends and to love their relations.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.

passages.text: He informed the people that the whites beyond the great water had killed their Maker, but he rose again; and he warned them that the whites would in some future day take possession of the Big Island, and it was impossible to prevent it: the red children would melt away like snow before the heat. The aged man, becoming sick, told them to get different kinds of roots to cure diseases, and showed them the manner of mourning. He died among them and was buried; but soon after, some person went to the grave and found he had risen, and he was never heard of since.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
